construction_notes: Patience index (expression 4): arithmetic mean over the five 8-weeks-versus-16-weeks choice situations of the share of the ten 100-point blocks saved for later receipt; range [0,1] in steps of 1/50; censored at both ends by construction, with 19 percent of subjects saving all blocks in all five situations.

Present/future bias: average over the five offered interest rates of the difference between the 0-8 week (short run) and 8-16 week (long run) savings choices; individuals are present biased if they save more in the long-run decisions.
Nonmonotonicity indicator: saving more in a choice situation offering a low interest rate than in a similar situation offering a high interest rate.
Risk aversion and altruism indices elicited with tasks and screens made as similar as possible to the patience task; both run from 0 to 1.
Wealth = value of real estate, deposits, stocks, bonds and mortgage deeds in deposit (and, in Table 1, cars and pension accounts) minus all debt except debt to private persons.

Tax-assessed house values adjusted by the average ratio of market prices to tax-assessed values among traded houses of the same property class, location and price range (following Leth-Petersen 2010).
Wealth rank = within cohort x time percentile rank; Table 2 panel A uses percentile ranks computed within cohorts in 2015; the DLSY arm uses the percentile rank in the sample.
Wealth amounts expressed in 1,000 DKK; the exchange rate at the time of the study was about 6.5 DKK per US dollar.
Credit constraint indicator: holding liquid assets worth less than one month of disposable income, measured in 2014 (the year before the wealth rank).

Marginal interest rate: imputed per account from yearly interest payments and end-of-year balances; highest debt-account rate for people with debt, lowest deposit-account rate for people without debt; measured in percent.
Stock returns: (dividend income + realized capital gains/losses) / market value of stocks, averaged over 2008-2014 and winsorized at the 5th and 95th percentiles.
Parental wealth measured when the respondent was 18 years old; initial wealth measured at age 18 (1983 for the DLSY sample, the first year of individual-level wealth data).
Education controls: 11 dummy indicators for years of completed education in the Figure 5 income regressions, 12 length-of-education indicators in Table 2.
Experimental payments: five choice situations between 8 and 16 weeks with rates of return of 5-25 percent (annualized 32-145 percent); payouts transferred to the subject's NemKonto.

claims.statement: A higher elicited patience index is associated with a higher percentile rank in the 2015 within-cohort wealth distribution (Table 2, panel A, column 1).

treatment.label: Patience (patience index elicited in the incentivized experiment)

definition.value: A simple patience index equal to the arithmetic mean of the share of 100-point blocks saved for later receipt across the five intertemporal choice situations with allocations between t1 = 8 weeks and t2 = 16 weeks: phi_patience = mean(z1/10, ..., z5/10), where zi is the number of blocks saved in situation i, so that phi_patience lies in [0,1] and takes values in steps of 1/50 (expression (4)). Higher values are interpreted as greater (long-run) patience. The index is censored at both ends by construction; 19 percent of individuals saved all blocks in all five situations.

timing.value: Elicited in the online experiment conducted in February 2015; payment dates were 'today', 'in 8 weeks' and 'in 16 weeks'.

outcome.label: wealth, rank (percentile rank in the within-cohort wealth distribution in 2015)

definition.value: The individual's percentile rank in the within cohort x time wealth distribution of the sample; Panel A of Table 2 uses percentile ranks in the wealth distribution computed within cohorts in 2015. Wealth is built from third-party reports to the Danish tax authorities: assets include bank deposits, market value of listed stocks, bonds and mortgage deeds in deposit, and the value of property assessed by the tax authorities, minus all debt except debt to private persons; tax-assessed house values are adjusted by the average market-price-to-tax-value ratio among traded houses of the same class, location and price range.

timing.value: Measured in 2015, the same year as the experiment.

units.value: wealth percentile ranks per unit of the patience index, i.e. the difference between the lowest (0) and the highest (1) level of patience

magnitude.interpretation: Moving from the lowest to the highest level of patience in the sample is associated with a difference of 11.4 wealth percentiles; the paper reports a p-value of 6.1 x 10^-11.

estimand.target_population: The experimental respondents born 1973-1983 who resided in the municipality of Copenhagen at age seven; the coefficient is the difference in the 2015 within-cohort wealth rank between the lowest and the highest level of patience observed in the sample.
estimand.time_horizon: wealth position measured in 2015, the same year in which patience was elicited

population.description: The 3,620 individuals who received a personal invitation, successfully completed the February 2015 online experiment and received a payment, linked to Danish administrative register data. (3,552 of them have non-missing values for the full control set.)
population.region: Denmark (sampled among individuals who resided in the municipality of Copenhagen when they were seven years old)
subgroups_defined: credit constrained (liquid assets worth less than one month's disposable income in 2014)
unconstrained (liquid assets worth more than one month's disposable income in 2014)
population.selection: Self-selection into the experiment: 27,613 individuals born 1973-1983 who resided in the municipality of Copenhagen at age seven were invited by letter; the 3,620 who completed the experiment and were paid (13 percent of invitees) form the sample.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation across individuals in behaviourally revealed time discounting, elicited in an incentivized money-sooner-or-later (convex time budget) online experiment run in February 2015 with 3,620 invited Copenhagen-born residents. No exogenous variation in preferences is available: the authors state that it is impossible in practice to randomly assign type characteristics to people.

key_assumptions.assumption: The experimentally elicited patience index measures the individual's subjective (long-run) time discounting rather than variation in real-life market interest rates, credit access or arbitrage opportunities
key_assumptions.supported_by: 15-year stability of the patience-wealth and patience-credit-constraint relationships; the association survives controlling for the marginal interest rate on liquidity and asset returns (Table 2, column 7); narrow-bracketing evidence of Andreoni et al. (2018)

key_assumptions.assumption: The association does not run from wealth to patience and is not generated by shocks that move both patience and wealth around the time patience is elicited
key_assumptions.supported_by: stability of the association over the 15-year period 2001-2015 and its reproduction with the 1973 DLSY survey measure of patience collected three decades before wealth is observed

key_assumptions.assumption: The 3,620 respondents who completed the experiment (13 percent of the 27,613 invitees) support the reported association despite self-selection into participation
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 comparison of respondents with a 10 percent random sample of the same birth cohorts; re-estimation with propensity-score weighting on register characteristics

key_assumptions.assumption: The association between wealth and the patience index is linear in the index, so that the single coefficient is the difference between the lowest and the highest level of patience in the sample

estimation.specification: Bivariate OLS regression of the 2015 within-cohort wealth percentile rank on the patience index; constant included but not reported (Table 2, panel A, column 1).
estimation.clustering: no clustering reported; robust (heteroskedasticity-consistent) standard errors in parentheses

heterogeneity.dimension: credit constraints (liquid assets below vs. above one month of disposable income in 2014)
heterogeneity.finding: The patience-wealth rank association is small and insignificant for credit constrained individuals (Table 2, panel A, column 5) and 11.1 percentiles for the unconstrained (column 6), considerably larger than the 8.5 percentiles for the full sample (column 3).

heterogeneity.dimension: position in the wealth distribution (quantile regressions, Figure 4)
heterogeneity.finding: The patience coefficient is close to 0 in the bottom 10 percent of the wealth distribution and rises to DKK 615,000 at percentile 95, about three times the average effect of DKK 215,000.

evidence.how: Looked for a confidence interval for this coefficient: Table 2 prints only the point estimate and the robust standard error in parentheses; no interval and no confidence level.

Looked for a baseline/control-group mean of the percentile-rank outcome: none is printed. Table 2 reports no outcome means, and the regressor is a continuous index with no control group. Table 1 reports the respondents' wealth distribution in levels (5th-95th percentiles) but no mean of the percentile rank.
Looked for the standard deviation of the outcome: neither Table 1, Table 2 nor Table 3 prints standard deviations; Table 1 reports distribution percentiles only.

Looked for a named register and register variable for the treatment: the paper names none. Patience is elicited in the authors' own online experiment (and, for Table 3, in the 1973 DLSY survey); the paper names no Statistics Denmark register variable for it.

Looked for a named register and register variable for the wealth outcome: the paper says only 'administrative register data at Statistics Denmark' based on third-party reports to the Danish tax authorities. No register short name (e.g. IND) and no variable name (e.g. PERINDKIALT) is printed anywhere in the paper.

Looked for a printed estimating equation for the regressions: the paper prints equations (1)-(3) for the theoretical life-cycle model and (4) for the patience index, but no estimating equation and no equation number for the wealth regressions. The specification is described only in prose and in the notes to Table 2.

Looked in the conclusion and introduction for a claim about the domain beyond the estimation sample over which this particular coefficient is asserted to hold: the authors make no such generalisation for this specification.
Looked for a pre-analysis plan, trial registration or AEA RCT registry number: the paper states none.
Looked for a statement of what would falsify the claim: the authors state none.

value.claimed_domain: Wealth formation and inequality beyond this sample: the authors claim the result points to the importance of incorporating heterogeneous time discounting into models of consumption and savings behavior, and that heterogeneity in preferences has a role to play in the formation of inequality.
boundary_conditions: the cross-sectional ordering of patience elicited under the relatively small experimental stakes must be the same as it would be under large stakes
the association is muted at the very bottom of the wealth distribution, where credit constraints bind

theory_referenced: standard savings theory: a basic deterministic life-cycle savings model in which patient people have more wealth at all points in the life cycle (Prediction 1)

definition.value: A simple patience index equal to the arithmetic mean of the share of 100-point blocks saved for later receipt across the five intertemporal choice situations with allocations between t1 = 8 weeks and t2 = 16 weeks: phi_patience = mean(z1/10, ..., z5/10), where zi is the number of blocks saved in situation i, so that phi_patience lies in [0,1] and takes values in steps of 1/50 (expression (4)). anchor_quote.text: In columns 5 and 6 of Table 2, we analyze the relationship between patience and wealth inequality for credit constrained individuals and unconstrained individuals, respectively.

claims.statement: A higher elicited patience index is associated with a higher percentile rank in the 2015 within-cohort wealth distribution (Table 2, panel A, column 6).

treatment.label: Patience (patience index elicited in the incentivized experiment)

definition.value: A simple patience index equal to the arithmetic mean of the share of 100-point blocks saved for later receipt across the five intertemporal choice situations with allocations between t1 = 8 weeks and t2 = 16 weeks: phi_patience = mean(z1/10, ..., z5/10), where zi is the number of blocks saved in situation i, so that phi_patience lies in [0,1] and takes values in steps of 1/50 (expression (4)). Higher values are interpreted as greater (long-run) patience. The index is censored at both ends by construction; 19 percent of individuals saved all blocks in all five situations.

timing.value: Elicited in the online experiment conducted in February 2015; payment dates were 'today', 'in 8 weeks' and 'in 16 weeks'.

outcome.label: wealth, rank (percentile rank in the within-cohort wealth distribution in 2015)

definition.value: The individual's percentile rank in the within cohort x time wealth distribution of the sample; Panel A of Table 2 uses percentile ranks in the wealth distribution computed within cohorts in 2015. Wealth is built from third-party reports to the Danish tax authorities: assets include bank deposits, market value of listed stocks, bonds and mortgage deeds in deposit, and the value of property assessed by the tax authorities, minus all debt except debt to private persons; tax-assessed house values are adjusted by the average market-price-to-tax-value ratio among traded houses of the same class, location and price range.

timing.value: Measured in 2015, the same year as the experiment.

units.value: wealth percentile ranks per unit of the patience index, i.e. the difference between the lowest (0) and the highest (1) level of patience

magnitude.interpretation: For individuals unlikely to be credit constrained the association is 11.1 percentiles, considerably larger than the 8.5 percentiles obtained for the full sample.

estimand.target_population: The experimental respondents born 1973-1983 who resided in the municipality of Copenhagen at age seven; the coefficient is the difference in the 2015 within-cohort wealth rank between the lowest and the highest level of patience observed in the sample.
estimand.time_horizon: wealth position measured in 2015, the same year in which patience was elicited

population.description: The 3,620 individuals who received a personal invitation, successfully completed the February 2015 online experiment and received a payment, linked to Danish administrative register data. claims.statement: A higher elicited patience index is associated with a higher level of net wealth in 2015, measured in amounts (1,000 DKK) (Table 2, panel B, column 1).

treatment.label: Patience (patience index elicited in the incentivized experiment)

definition.value: A simple patience index equal to the arithmetic mean of the share of 100-point blocks saved for later receipt across the five intertemporal choice situations with allocations between t1 = 8 weeks and t2 = 16 weeks: phi_patience = mean(z1/10, ..., z5/10), where zi is the number of blocks saved in situation i, so that phi_patience lies in [0,1] and takes values in steps of 1/50 (expression (4)). Higher values are interpreted as greater (long-run) patience. The index is censored at both ends by construction; 19 percent of individuals saved all blocks in all five situations.

timing.value: Elicited in the online experiment conducted in February 2015; payment dates were 'today', 'in 8 weeks' and 'in 16 weeks'.

outcome.label: wealth, amounts (1,000 DKK)

definition.value: Net wealth measured in amounts (1,000 DKK) in 2015: third-party reported assets (bank deposits, market value of listed stocks, bonds and mortgage deeds in deposit, tax-assessed property values adjusted toward market values) minus all debt except debt to private persons.

timing.value: Measured in 2015, the same year as the experiment.

units.value: 1,000 DKK of net wealth per unit of the patience index, i.e. the difference between the lowest (0) and the highest (1) level of patience

magnitude.interpretation: Moving from the lowest to the highest level of patience is associated with DKK 215,000 more wealth, about half of the median wealth level reported in Table 1.

estimand.target_population: The experimental respondents born 1973-1983 who resided in the municipality of Copenhagen at age seven; the coefficient is the difference in 2015 net wealth (1,000 DKK) between the lowest and the highest level of patience observed in the sample.
estimand.time_horizon: wealth position measured in 2015, the same year in which patience was elicited

population.description: The 3,620 individuals who received a personal invitation, successfully completed the February 2015 online experiment and received a payment, linked to Danish administrative register data. (3,552 of them have non-missing values for the full control set.)
population.region: Denmark (sampled among individuals who resided in the municipality of Copenhagen when they were seven years old)
subgroups_defined: credit constrained (liquid assets worth less than one month's disposable income in 2014)

population.selection: Self-selection into the experiment: 27,613 individuals born 1973-1983 who resided in the municipality of Copenhagen at age seven were invited by letter; the 3,620 who completed the experiment and were paid (13 percent of invitees) form the sample.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation across individuals in behaviourally revealed time discounting, elicited in an incentivized money-sooner-or-later (convex time budget) online experiment run in February 2015 with 3,620 invited Copenhagen-born residents. definition.value: A simple patience index equal to the arithmetic mean of the share of 100-point blocks saved for later receipt across the five intertemporal choice situations with allocations between t1 = 8 weeks and t2 = 16 weeks: phi_patience = mean(z1/10, ..., z5/10), where zi is the number of blocks saved in situation i, so that phi_patience lies in [0,1] and takes values in steps of 1/50 (expression (4)). ambiguities: Statistical significance left null: the paper does not state it for this coefficient and the ratio of the printed coefficient to the printed robust standard error (5.31/2.70) is right at the conventional 5 percent boundary, so a careful reader could classify it either way.

evidence.how: Looked for a confidence interval for this coefficient: Table 2 prints only the point estimate and the robust standard error in parentheses; no interval and no confidence level.
Looked for a p-value for this coefficient: Table 2 prints no p-values and no significance stars; only robust standard errors in parentheses.

Looked for a baseline/control-group mean of the percentile-rank outcome: none is printed. Table 2 reports no outcome means, and the regressor is a continuous index with no control group. Table 1 reports the respondents' wealth distribution in levels (5th-95th percentiles) but no mean of the percentile rank.
Looked for the standard deviation of the outcome: neither Table 1, Table 2 nor Table 3 prints standard deviations; Table 1 reports distribution percentiles only.

Looked for a named register and register variable for the treatment: the paper names none. Patience is elicited in the authors' own online experiment (and, for Table 3, in the 1973 DLSY survey); the paper names no Statistics Denmark register variable for it.

Looked for a named register and register variable for the wealth outcome: the paper says only 'administrative register data at Statistics Denmark' based on third-party reports to the Danish tax authorities. No register short name (e.g. IND) and no variable name (e.g. PERINDKIALT) is printed anywhere in the paper.

Looked for a printed estimating equation for the regressions: the paper prints equations (1)-(3) for the theoretical life-cycle model and (4) for the patience index, but no estimating equation and no equation number for the wealth regressions. The specification is described only in prose and in the notes to Table 2.

Looked in the conclusion and introduction for a claim about the domain beyond the estimation sample over which this particular coefficient is asserted to hold: the authors make no such generalisation for this specification.
Looked for a pre-analysis plan, trial registration or AEA RCT registry number: the paper states none.
Looked for a statement of what would falsify the claim: the authors state none.

claims.statement: Interest rate on liquidity (the marginal interest rate, percent) is associated with the percentile rank in the 2015 within-cohort wealth distribution (Table 2, panel A, column 7).

treatment.label: Interest rate on liquidity (the marginal interest rate, percent)

definition.value: The interest rate on marginal liquidity, imputed from account-level register data on debt, deposits and interest payments during the year: for each account the interest rate is imputed from yearly interest payments and end-of-year balances; for people with debt accounts the highest interest rate among debt accounts is taken, for people without debt the lowest interest rate among their deposit accounts. Measured in percent.

timing.value: measured from account-level data for the year; included as a control in column 7

outcome.label: wealth, rank (percentile rank in the within-cohort wealth distribution in 2015)

definition.value: The individual's percentile rank in the within cohort x time wealth distribution of the sample; Panel A of Table 2 uses percentile ranks in the wealth distribution computed within cohorts in 2015. Wealth is built from third-party reports to the Danish tax authorities: assets include bank deposits, market value of listed stocks, bonds and mortgage deeds in deposit, and the value of property assessed by the tax authorities, minus all debt except debt to private persons; tax-assessed house values are adjusted by the average market-price-to-tax-value ratio among traded houses of the same class, location and price range.

timing.value: Measured in 2015, the same year as the experiment.

units.value: wealth percentile ranks per percentage point

magnitude.interpretation: A one percentage point higher interest rate on marginal liquidity is associated with a 1.63 lower wealth percentile rank; the coefficient is precisely estimated and has the expected negative sign.

estimand.target_population: The experimental respondents entering column 7 of Table 2 (N = 2157); the coefficient is the partial association of Interest rate on liquidity (the marginal interest rate, percent) with the 2015 wealth rank given the other regressors in the column.
estimand.time_horizon: wealth position measured in 2015

population.description: The 3,620 individuals who received a personal invitation, successfully completed the February 2015 online experiment and received a payment, linked to Danish administrative register data. treatment.label: Rate of return on stocks, 2008-2014

definition.value: Individual stock market return, computed by dividing the sum of dividend income and realized capital gains/losses during the year by the market value of stocks, averaged over 2008-2014 and winsorized at the 5th and 95th percentiles; measured in percent.

timing.value: average over 2008-2014, before the 2015 wealth measurement

outcome.label: wealth, rank (percentile rank in the within-cohort wealth distribution in 2015)

definition.value: The individual's percentile rank in the within cohort x time wealth distribution of the sample; Panel A of Table 2 uses percentile ranks in the wealth distribution computed within cohorts in 2015. Wealth is built from third-party reports to the Danish tax authorities: assets include bank deposits, market value of listed stocks, bonds and mortgage deeds in deposit, and the value of property assessed by the tax authorities, minus all debt except debt to private persons; tax-assessed house values are adjusted by the average market-price-to-tax-value ratio among traded houses of the same class, location and price range.

timing.value: Measured in 2015, the same year as the experiment.

units.value: wealth percentile ranks per percentage point

magnitude.interpretation: Given the other covariates, the return on assets turns out not to be important for the wealth rank: the coefficient is 0.36 with a robust standard error of 0.54.

claims.statement: Respondents in the high patience group of the 1973 DLSY time-discounting question hold a higher percentile rank in the wealth distribution in 2001 than the Low patience reference group (Table 3, column 1).

treatment.label: High patience group (1973 DLSY survey measure of time discounting)

definition.value: Indicator for the high patience group, defined by the answer given in the 1973 Danish Longitudinal Survey of Youth to the question which of three jobs the respondent would choose: (i) average salary from the start, (ii) low salary the first two years but high salary later, (iii) very low salary the first four years but later very high salary. Respondents answering (iii) are High patience (727 respondents), (ii) Medium patience (1,157) and (i) Low patience (664, the omitted reference group). The authors interpret the preference over the timing of income streams as a proxy for time discounting.

timing.value: Elicited in the 1973 DLSY survey, when respondents were 18-21 years old.

outcome.label: wealth, Rank (percentile rank in the wealth distribution in 2001)

definition.value: The individual's percentile rank in the wealth distribution of the DLSY sample in 2001; the dependent variable in columns 1-2 of Table 3. Wealth is the register-based measure described for the core analysis (third-party reported assets minus debt except debt to private persons).

timing.value: Measured in 2001, the first year of panel A of Figure 6, when the 1952-1955 cohorts were in their mid-lifes.

units.value: wealth percentiles relative to the Low patience reference group

magnitude.interpretation: Respondents who in 1973 preferred the steepest salary profile are 7.71 wealth percentiles higher in the 2001 wealth distribution than those who preferred a flat profile; the difference is significant at the 1 percent level.

estimand.target_population: DLSY respondents from the 1952-1955 birth cohorts who answered the 1973 time-discounting question; the coefficient is the 2001 wealth gap between the high patience group and the Low patience group.
estimand.time_horizon: wealth measured in 2001, 28 years after the 1973 survey measure of patience (the paper's section heading describes it as 'Three Decades Later')

population.period: patience measured in the 1973 survey; wealth measured in 2001

definition.value: Indicator for the high patience group, defined by the answer given in the 1973 Danish Longitudinal Survey of Youth to the question which of three jobs the respondent would choose: (i) average salary from the start, (ii) low salary the first two years but high salary later, (iii) very low salary the first four years but later very high salary. Respondents answering (iii) are High patience (727 respondents), (ii) Medium patience (1,157) and (i) Low patience (664, the omitted reference group). The authors interpret the preference over the timing of income streams as a proxy for time discounting.

timing.value: Elicited in the 1973 DLSY survey, when respondents were 18-21 years old.

outcome.label: wealth, Rank (percentile rank in the wealth distribution in 2001)

definition.value: The individual's percentile rank in the wealth distribution of the DLSY sample in 2001; the dependent variable in columns 1-2 of Table 3. Wealth is the register-based measure described for the core analysis (third-party reported assets minus debt except debt to private persons).

timing.value: Measured in 2001, the first year of panel A of Figure 6, when the 1952-1955 cohorts were in their mid-lifes.

units.value: wealth percentiles relative to the Low patience reference group

magnitude.interpretation: With controls the high patience group parameter is still sizable, 3.24 percentiles, and significant at a five percent level.

estimand.target_population: DLSY respondents from the 1952-1955 birth cohorts who answered the 1973 time-discounting question; the coefficient is the 2001 wealth gap between the high patience group and the Low patience group.
estimand.time_horizon: wealth measured in 2001, 28 years after the 1973 survey measure of patience (the paper's section heading describes it as 'Three Decades Later')

population.description: 2,548 respondents of the Danish Longitudinal Survey of Youth (DLSY) from the 1952-1955 birth cohorts who answered the 1973 time-discounting question, merged with administrative register data; 2,546 enter the regressions (two observations dropped for missing 1983 wealth data).
population.ages: 18-21 at the 1973 survey; about 45-60 over the 2001-2015 wealth period
population.period: patience measured in the 1973 survey; wealth measured in 2001
population.region: Denmark
population.selection: DLSY survey respondents from the 1952-1955 cohorts who answered the 1973 time-discounting question and could be merged with register data; two observations dropped for missing 1983 wealth.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation in the answer given in 1973, at ages 18-21, to a Danish Longitudinal Survey of Youth question about the preferred timing of a salary profile, linked to register wealth 28 years later. No exogenous variation in preferences is claimed.

key_assumptions.assumption: The 1973 DLSY question about the preferred timing of a salary profile proxies time discounting, with respondents choosing the steepest profile the most patient and those choosing a flat profile the least patient
key_assumptions.supported_by: the authors report a strong correlation between the survey-based measure of patience and patience elicited in the incentivized experiment for a subsample of experiment participants who were also asked the survey question (online Appendix D.1); the authors call the survey measure 'a crude measure of time discounting'

key_assumptions.assumption: Because patience is measured in 1973, three decades before wealth is observed, the association cannot run from wealth to patience and cannot be generated by shocks moving both around the time patience is elicited
key_assumptions.supported_by: temporal precedence of the 1973 survey measure and the authors' own reading of the Table 3 / Figure 6 results

key_assumptions.assumption: The 2,546 DLSY respondents who answered the 1973 time-discounting question and could be merged with register data support the reported association
key_assumptions.supported_by: the authors report the sample size (2,548 respondents, 82 percent from the 1954 cohort) and that two observations are dropped because of missing 1983 wealth data; no further selection correction is reported

implies_edges.from: answering the 1973 DLSY time-discounting question and being merged to registers

key_assumptions.assumption: The association is captured by group indicators for medium and high patience relative to the low patience reference group, imposing no ordering or linearity within groups

Conditional on educational attainment, income deciles, initial wealth in 1983 and demographics, the remaining patience-group differences in wealth reflect the savings channel rather than other wealth determinants
key_assumptions.supported_by: the controls listed in the notes to Table 3; the authors note that including the controls mutes the patience coefficients

rhs: remaining (unobserved) determinants of wealth in 2001
given: year indicators for educational attainment
income decile indicators based on the position in the gross income (excluding capital income) distribution
initial wealth decile indicators based on the position in the wealth distribution in 1983
a gender dummy
a dummy for being single
a dummy for having dependent children

threats_discussed: reverse causality from wealth to patience
shocks affecting both patience and wealth around the time patience is elicited
crudeness of the survey measure of time discounting
no parent-child link available for cohorts born before 1960, so parental wealth cannot be controlled for
robustness_checks: this specification is itself the robustness check for the experimental results, using a survey measure elicited three decades earlier
comparison with the education-wealth association in Figure 6 panel B
unresolved_confounders: parental wealth, which cannot be controlled for because the identity of most parents is missing in the register data for cohorts born before 1960

controls: year indicators for educational attainment

estimation.clustering: no clustering reported; robust (heteroskedasticity-consistent) standard errors in parentheses

Looked for a p-value for this coefficient: Table 3 prints no p-values and no significance stars; only robust standard errors in parentheses.

Looked for the mean of the outcome in the omitted Low patience group: Table 3 prints no group means. Figure 6 panel A plots the Low patience group's average wealth percentile rank but prints no numerical value.
Looked for the standard deviation of the outcome in the DLSY sample: Table 3 and the surrounding text print none.

Looked for a named register and register variable for the treatment: the paper names none. Patience is elicited in the authors' own online experiment (and, for Table 3, in the 1973 DLSY survey); the paper names no Statistics Denmark register variable for it.

treatment.label: Patience (patience index elicited in the incentivized experiment)

definition.value: A simple patience index equal to the arithmetic mean of the share of 100-point blocks saved for later receipt across the five intertemporal choice situations with allocations between t1 = 8 weeks and t2 = 16 weeks: phi_patience = mean(z1/10, ..., z5/10), where zi is the number of blocks saved in situation i, so that phi_patience lies in [0,1] and takes values in steps of 1/50 (expression (4)). units.value: DKK of wealth per percentage point of the annual discount rate

magnitude.interpretation: The association between wealth levels and discount rates is in the range DKK -918 to DKK -720 per percentage point across the four models; the abstract-level summary in footnote 2 states that a one standard deviation higher discount rate implies a decrease in wealth of DKK 38,700-46,900.

estimand.target_population: The experimental respondents; the quantity is the association between wealth in DKK and the structurally estimated individual discount rate.
estimand.time_horizon: wealth measured in 2015, the year of the experiment

population.description: The 3,620 individuals who received a personal invitation, successfully completed the February 2015 online experiment and received a payment, linked to Danish administrative register data. (3,552 of them have non-missing values for the full control set.)
population.region: Denmark (sampled among individuals who resided in the municipality of Copenhagen when they were seven years old)
subgroups_defined: credit constrained (liquid assets worth less than one month's disposable income in 2014)
unconstrained (liquid assets worth more than one month's disposable income in 2014)
population.selection: Self-selection into the experiment: 27,613 individuals born 1973-1983 who resided in the municipality of Copenhagen at age seven were invited by letter; the 3,620 who completed the experiment and were paid (13 percent of invitees) form the sample.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation across individuals in behaviourally revealed time discounting, elicited in an incentivized money-sooner-or-later (convex time budget) online experiment run in February 2015 with 3,620 invited Copenhagen-born residents. No exogenous variation in preferences is available: the authors state that it is impossible in practice to randomly assign type characteristics to people.

key_assumptions.assumption: The experimentally elicited patience index measures the individual's subjective (long-run) time discounting rather than variation in real-life market interest rates, credit access or arbitrage opportunities
key_assumptions.supported_by: 15-year stability of the patience-wealth and patience-credit-constraint relationships; the association survives controlling for the marginal interest rate on liquidity and asset returns (Table 2, column 7); narrow-bracketing evidence of Andreoni et al. (2018)

key_assumptions.assumption: The association does not run from wealth to patience and is not generated by shocks that move both patience and wealth around the time patience is elicited
key_assumptions.supported_by: stability of the association over the 15-year period 2001-2015 and its reproduction with the 1973 DLSY survey measure of patience collected three decades before wealth is observed

key_assumptions.assumption: The 3,620 respondents who completed the experiment (13 percent of the 27,613 invitees) support the reported association despite self-selection into participation
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 comparison of respondents with a 10 percent random sample of the same birth cohorts; re-estimation with propensity-score weighting on register characteristics

key_assumptions.assumption: The association is captured by group indicators for medium and high patience relative to the low patience reference group, imposing no ordering or linearity within groups
The association between wealth and the patience index is linear in the index, so that the single coefficient is the difference between the lowest and the highest level of patience in the sample

threats_discussed: reverse causality: wealth causing elicited patience
elicited time discounting reflecting market interest rates, credit constraints or arbitrage rather than subjective time preference
short-term income or wealth shocks around the time patience is elicited affecting both patience and wealth
selection into experiment participation (3,620 of 27,613 invitees, 13 percent)
measurement error in wealth (tax-assessed housing values; pension and car wealth only from 2014)
correlation between patience and other wealth determinants (permanent income, income profile, initial wealth, parental transfers, risk preferences)
robustness_checks: patience measures built from all other combinations of the payment dates ('today', 'in 8 weeks', 'in 16 weeks') give very similar estimates (online Appendix D.2)
re-estimation on a subsample omitting the 19 percent who always postpone payments: association somewhat smaller but still quantitatively important and strongly significant
structurally estimated discount rates from a random utility model, ranked and used as regressor: close to 11 rank points from least to most patient
tax-assessed house values adjusted toward market values: association nearly unchanged
inclusion of car values and of pension wealth (available from 2014): estimates within two standard errors of the baseline
household-level instead of individual-level wealth: association almost unchanged
three-, five- and seven-year averages of wealth and income: coefficient on patience essentially identical
subsamples with stable relationships and no unemployment or health shocks before elicitation
subsample where both parents are alive in 2015 (rules out inheritance)
more detailed education controls beyond the 11/12 length-of-education dummies
propensity-score weighting on register characteristics to address selection into the experiment
replication with the 1973 DLSY survey measure of patience (Table 3, Figure 6)
unresolved_confounders: all other wealth determinants correlated with patience -- permanent income, the time profile of income, initial wealth, wealth transfers from parents, and risk preferences -- which the bivariate association does not hold fixed

estimator.value: OLS (regression of wealth in amounts on individual discount rates)

estimation.specification: Regression of wealth in amounts on individual discount rates estimated from four different random utility models; reported in footnote 11 on page 1191 and in online Appendix Section C.1.

source_table.value: Footnote 11 on page 1191, reporting results from online Appendix Section C.1 (no main-text table or figure)

ambiguities: The footnote reports a range across four models rather than one coefficient, and reports no standard errors, so point estimate, uncertainty and significance are all left null.

evidence.how: The estimate is reported only in footnote 11 on page 1191 and in online Appendix Section C.1; there is no main-text table or figure for it, so no digest exhibit id applies.
Looked for a single point estimate: the footnote reports a range across four random utility models (DKK -918 to DKK -720 per percentage point), not one number, so no point estimate is transcribed.
Looked for a standard error, confidence interval or p-value: the footnote reports none.
Looked for the number of observations in this regression: the footnote does not state it.

Looked for a baseline/control-group mean of wealth in levels: Table 1 prints the respondents' wealth distribution by percentile (median DKK 486,006) but no mean, and Table 2 prints no outcome mean. The text compares the DKK 215,000 coefficient to 'about half of the median wealth level reported in Table 1'.
Looked for the standard deviation of the outcome: neither Table 1, Table 2 nor Table 3 prints standard deviations; Table 1 reports distribution percentiles only.

Looked for a named register and register variable for the treatment: the paper names none. Patience is elicited in the authors' own online experiment (and, for Table 3, in the 1973 DLSY survey); the paper names no Statistics Denmark register variable for it.

Looked for a named register and register variable for the wealth outcome: the paper says only 'administrative register data at Statistics Denmark' based on third-party reports to the Danish tax authorities. No register short name (e.g. IND) and no variable name (e.g. PERINDKIALT) is printed anywhere in the paper.

Looked for a printed estimating equation for the regressions: the paper prints equations (1)-(3) for the theoretical life-cycle model and (4) for the patience index, but no estimating equation and no equation number for the wealth regressions. The specification is described only in prose and in the notes to Table 2.

Looked in the conclusion and introduction for a claim about the domain beyond the estimation sample over which this particular coefficient is asserted to hold: the authors make no such generalisation for this specification.
Looked for a pre-analysis plan, trial registration or AEA RCT registry number: the paper states none.
Looked for a statement of what would falsify the claim: the authors state none.

theory_referenced: standard savings theory: a higher rate of time preference lowers wealth at all points in the life cycle (Prediction 1)
outcomes_examined_not_reported: financial wealth (a narrower wealth concept): the paper says it finds a larger association with patience, but the estimate is reported only in online Appendix D.2
household-level wealth: examined, reported only in online Appendix D.2
wealth including pension accounts and car values: examined, reported only in online Appendix D.2
propensity to be credit constrained, 2001-2015: examined, reported only in online Appendix C.3
savings propensities and the wealth gap over the life cycle from age 18 to 40: examined, reported only in online Appendix C.2
structurally estimated individual discount rates from four random utility models: examined, reported only in online Appendix B.3 and C.1
